title: Compare doubles the safe way

blocks.text: `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `false` in Java: most decimal fractions have no exact binary form, so a sum carries a tiny rounding error. Comparing floating-point numbers with `==` is therefore a bug.
Write `NearlyEqual.nearlyEqual(double a, double b)`. It returns `true` when the two values differ by **less than** `NearlyEqual.EPSILON` (`1e-9`), and `false` otherwise.

items: `Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY` is nearly equal to itself (and to nothing else), and the same holds for negative infinity. Note that `Infinity - Infinity` is `NaN`.
`Double.NaN` is nearly equal to **nothing**, not even to itself, just as `NaN == NaN` is `false`.

cases.says: Sums with a rounding error compare equal within the tolerance.
Values a millionth apart are not equal: the tolerance is 1e-9.
An infinity is nearly equal to itself, although Infinity - Infinity is NaN.
NaN is nearly equal to nothing, not even to NaN.

concepts: Floating-point values are compared with a tolerance, never with ==.
NaN and the infinities behave specially in comparisons.
